source: MAFF Department of Agricultural Extension / ASPIRE Project, IFAD-funded - "ដំណាំក្រូចថ្លុង" (Pomelo Cultivation Guide), 2017, 90pp
text:
Foot rot / Phytophthora rot (ជម្ងឺហ្វូវ ឬ ជម្ងឺឡុយពណ៌ត្នោត, Foot Rot, caused by Phytophthora species) is one of the most serious citrus diseases described in the source, capable of attacking multiple parts of the tree: the root system, the trunk collar/foot of the tree, foliage (as a blight), and fruit (as a brown rot). It thrives in wet, poorly drained soil and spreads readily where water splashes soil onto the lower trunk or where the graft union sits too close to the soil line.

At the foot/collar, infection shows as darkened, sunken, often gummy bark lesions at the base of the trunk that can girdle and kill the tree if they encircle the trunk; on roots, infection causes rot and dieback of the root system, weakening the tree's ability to take up water and nutrients; on foliage and fruit, wet weather can spread Phytophthora spores that cause blighted leaves and brown, rotting fruit, especially fruit low in the canopy near the ground.

Prevention is the primary defense, since Phytophthora is difficult to eliminate once established: planting on well-drained soil, choosing Phytophthora-tolerant rootstock (the source names trifoliate orange and Fortunella/kumquat-type rootstocks as more tolerant options), keeping the graft union well above the soil line, avoiding soil and mulch contact with the trunk, and improving drainage around the tree base. Where infection is found, treatment includes cutting away and disinfecting affected bark, applying copper fungicide or Bordeaux mixture to wounds and to the trunk base, and drenching soil around affected roots with an appropriate fungicide.
